The sun is setting again. Sitting in the armchair by the window, I like to watch the reddish and orange hues that form over the rooftops. Of course, now I can’t see as well as before. I wanted to crochet, and they convinced me to have cataract surgery: “You’ll be able to crochet again,” they said. The truth is, I can’t crochet, but I don’t miss it either. I don’t feel like crocheting.

Instead, I sit here and watch the sun set, trying to appreciate its colors, but I barely can. Instead, I try to remember them. My eyes have scanned this landscape so many times, so many years in the same house... I can imagine those colors day after day, the cool evening air coming in through the window and moving the curtains. Before I know it, my eyes are closed.

This is what my life has become in recent years—I close my eyes often, recalling other times, not necessarily better ones. My life has never been a bed of roses. The walls of this house contain laughter and tears; this house has endured so many years with me inside.

I never liked going out much; my husband, may he rest in peace, used to complain about it, and now my son does too. Yes, I’m ninety-one years old, he says, but thank God, I still have my wits and some physical strength. Lucidity, he says.

And what do I want my lucidity for? To realize how the world changes until I no longer understand it? To see how the people I loved for so long have been gone for years? I’m tired of living.

The girl who looks after me at night will arrive soon. Well, “looks after” is a way of putting it, because she spends the night watching TV, using electricity (which I have to pay for), and if I need her help one day, she barely hears me when I call. Not that I have much strength to raise my voice. Or the desire.

My son says she takes good care of me and that I can’t complain because I’ve been very lucky with her. I liked that Romanian girl who left... Who knows where she is, dead or in jail. It was her husband’s fault, that wicked man who made her do despicable things. It’s true she stole quite a bit of money in jewelry, but it wasn’t her fault; it was her husband. If she came back, I would forgive her. She was good, unlike this girl who comes now with four or five dogs at home. That’s not natural.

This Saturday, my granddaughter will come to see me. She’s coming with her boyfriend, a good man. But from what she tells me, I think she wants to have children with him. She doesn’t know what she’s saying. She’s going to complicate her life; children only bring problems—that’s why I only had one.

Now that the end is near, I feel like I’ve suffered more than I should have... Always worrying about others, my husband, my grandchildren... Now I just want the suffering to end. I no longer know what is real and what I imagine, but I spend so many hours alone at home that it’s hard to distinguish.

Sometimes, I remember better times, the few I’ve lived, and I smile with my eyes closed. Times when we sat around the table to eat, and everyone smiled. Until the table stopped smiling and I could no longer make more soup, salad, and tomato bread to bring back their smiles. Its coldness entered my body and stayed there forever. Until the end of time.
